Open a new level with score 0

Add the closed group to its parent

p: An empty pair `()` closes with `v = 0`, and `2·0` would be 0, but its score is 1. For a non-empty pair, `v ≥ 1`, so `2·v` is always at least 2 and wins the max. A single rule handles both cases.

bullets: Space: O(depth) for the stack (O(n) worst case).

856.takeaway: Stack of level scores: on ')' close the level with max(2·inner, 1) and add it to the parent.

p: A swap changes at most two positions. With 0 differences the strings are already equal, so the swap must be a no-op (needs a repeated letter). 859.takeaway: Count the mismatches: 0 needs a repeated letter, 2 must be a mirrored pair, anything else fails.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Prefix sums: `pre[i]` = sum of the first i numbers
Candidate start positions with increasing prefix sums
A monotonic deque; store indexes to compute lengths
The oldest candidate already gives a valid subarray
Record the length, then drop it: any later end would only be longer
A newer start with a smaller or equal prefix beats older ones
Newer = shorter, smaller prefix = larger sum: the old candidate can never be better
Replaced by −1 at the end if still `inf`

blocks.h: Why not a normal sliding window?
p: A two-pointer window needs non-negative numbers: shrinking must always reduce the sum. With negatives the sum can go up when you remove elements, so the usual window logic is wrong. The monotonic deque on prefix sums handles negatives by discarding provably useless start positions.

bullets: Time: O(n): each index enters and leaves the deque once.

862.takeaway: Monotonic deque on prefix sums: pop from the front while the sum reaches k, and from the back while prefixes are not smaller.

Two pieces of information from one traversal
The deepest nodes are only on the left
Deepest nodes on both sides (or this node is a leaf)
This node is the lowest common ancestor of the deepest nodes

p: Tree `[3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4]` → node 2 (subtree 2,7,4). Nodes are finished bottom-up:

If one side is strictly deeper, every deepest node lies there, so the answer is entirely inside that side. If both sides have the same depth, deepest nodes occur in both, so the smallest subtree that contains them all must be rooted at the current node. This is also the lowest common ancestor of the deepest leaves.

865.takeaway: Return (depth, answer) from each subtree: the deeper side wins, and equal depths make the current node the answer.

Distance equals the fuel you could have in total
Add all reachable stations to the pool, but don't stop yet
Max-heap of the fuel amounts of passed stations
Stop at the station with the most fuel
Delayed decision: refuel only when you would otherwise run out

p: Every station you drove past could have been used. When the tank would run dry you pick, in hindsight, the station with the most fuel among those you passed, since each stop costs the same and the largest refuel gets the farthest. This greedy choice gives the minimum number of stops.

871.takeaway: Delayed greedy with a max-heap: collect passed stations, and refuel at the biggest one only when you cannot go further.

p: `[5,3,4,5]`. `dp[i][j]` for interval i..j (upper triangle):

blocks.h: Why does the colouring decide the answer?
p: Splitting into two groups with no dislike inside a group is exactly 2-colouring the graph (a bipartite check). A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle; BFS colouring finds an odd cycle as an edge between two nodes of the same colour. The triangle is the shortest odd cycle.

886.takeaway: Bipartite check: BFS (Breadth-First Search) 2-colouring; an edge joining equal colours means an odd cycle, so the answer is False.

blocks.h: Why is the tree not unique in general, and what does this code assume?
p: When a node has exactly one child, preorder and postorder cannot tell whether the child is left or right. The code treats `preorder[i+1]` as the left child's root, so a lone child always becomes the left child (allowed by the problem).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: value → how many copies are in the stack
A stack of values that have reached frequency f (in push order)
One value appears in groups 1…its frequency; the latest push to a level is on top
The pop always comes from this group
Most recent value among the most frequent
Tie-break by recency comes from the group being a stack
Move down when the level is empty
Frequencies change by exactly one, so the next level is `top − 1`

p: push 5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5, then pop four times (answers: 5, 7, 5, 4):

Pushing 5 a second time puts it in group 2 as well as group 1, so the group at the highest level lists exactly the values with that frequency, in push order. Popping from there returns the most frequent, most recent value, and removing it leaves it correctly in lower groups (with frequency reduced). No searching or heap is needed.

bullets: Time: O(1) per push and pop.

895.takeaway: Frequency-bucketed stacks: group[f] holds values that reached frequency f in push order; pop from the highest non-empty group.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: List of `(price, span)` with strictly decreasing prices
Each entry stands for a block of consecutive days it already absorbed
Earlier price is not higher than today's
Those days belong to today's span
Use the stored span instead of walking back day by day
A later higher price can absorb this block in O(1)

blocks.h: Why store spans in the stack?
p: Without spans you would pop and then still have to count the days those entries represent. Each entry's span already counts all earlier days it dominated, so adding it counts them at once. Each price is pushed and popped once, giving O(1) amortised time.

901.takeaway: Monotonic stack of (price, span): absorb all earlier prices ≤ today and add their spans.

`len(cnt)` is the number of kinds (baskets used)
Window needs more than two baskets
Shrink from the left until only two kinds remain
Number of trees in the window

blocks.h: Why is this 'longest window with at most 2 distinct values'?
p: Two baskets with one kind each means the picked trees contain at most two kinds, and they must be consecutive. That is exactly the longest subarray with at most two distinct values. It is the same sliding window as 'longest substring with at most k distinct characters' with k = 2.

904.takeaway: Sliding window with a counter: longest subarray with at most two distinct values.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of positions to the left (including i) where `arr[i]` is the minimum, i.e. distance to the previous strictly smaller element
Choices for the subarray's left end
Distance to the next smaller-or-equal element
Strict on one side, non-strict on the other
Breaks ties so equal minima are counted once per subarray
Contribution: value × number of subarrays where it is the minimum

p: Instead of enumerating all O(n²) subarrays, ask for each element: in how many subarrays is it the minimum? If it can extend `left` steps to the left and `right` steps to the right before meeting a smaller element, it is the minimum of left × right subarrays. For the 1 at index 1: left = 2 (it can start at 0 or 1), right = 3, giving 6 subarrays × 1.

blocks.h: Why `>` on one side and `>=` on the other?
p: With equal values, for example `[2,2]`, both could claim the same subarray as theirs. Treating equals as 'smaller' only on one side assigns each subarray to exactly one minimum (the leftmost or rightmost occurrence).

907.takeaway: Contribution technique: for each element count the subarrays where it is the minimum using nearest-smaller distances from monotonic stacks.

Range with no change in relative spread (all +k or all −k)
Largest number overall, in the −k group

p: Adding +k to a small number and −k to a large number brings them closer. In a sorted array, if a larger element got +k while a smaller one got −k, swapping their signs never makes the range wider. So the optimum is a prefix with +k followed by a suffix with −k, and trying every split point i (O(n)) finds it.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) from the sort.

910.takeaway: Sort, give the prefix +k and the suffix −k, and try every split point.

Slice of up to three cells above: columns j−1, j, j+1
`max(…, 0)` stops the left index becoming −1 (which would wrap around); the slice end is clipped automatically

p: For j = 0, `dp[j-1:j+2]` would be `dp[-1:2]`, which in Python is an empty slice (start −1 means the last index), silently losing the valid neighbours. Clamping the start to 0 gives `dp[0:2]`. The right edge needs no guard because slices past the end are clipped.

bullets: Space: O(n) for one row at a time.

931.takeaway: Row-by-row DP: each cell adds the cheapest of the (up to three) cells above; clamp the left index at 0.

Seed the BFS (Breadth-First Search) with all cells of island 1 at distance 0
Multi-source BFS: the search expands outward from the whole island at once
The second island must stay untouched so the BFS can reach it
Reached land that is not in `seen`
That is the second island, and `d` is the number of water cells crossed

p: `[[0,1,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]]`: DFS (Depth-First Search) marks the island at [(0, 1)]. Then BFS expands outward; answer 2:

head: Popped (r, c)
Distance d
What happens
rows: neighbour (2, 2) is land of the other island → return 2

blocks.h: Why DFS first and BFS second?
p: DFS identifies one whole island so it can serve as the BFS source set. BFS from all of its cells gives distances in water layers; the first land cell found outside `seen` belongs to the other island, and BFS guarantees the layer count is minimal. `d` counts the water cells that must be flipped.

934.takeaway: Find one island with DFS, then multi-source BFS outward; the first layer that touches land of the other island is the answer.

p: Result False: after `1` and `2` are on the stack the top is 2, but the next expected pop is 1, so the stack is stuck with elements left.

Popping the top when it equals the next expected value never hurts: if you delayed, anything pushed afterwards would cover it and make that pop impossible. So pop as soon as the expected value is at the top.

946.takeaway: Simulate the stack: push each value, then pop while the top equals the next expected popped value; success means the stack ends empty.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Visit nodes level by level, left to right
So gaps appear in the traversal order
A gap has already been seen
In a complete tree every real node comes before the first gap
A real node after a gap
The last level is not filled from the left

p: `[1,2,3,4,5,6]` → True (every `None` comes after all real nodes). For `[1,2,3,4,5,null,7]` → False:

blocks.h: Why must `None` children go into the queue?
p: Completeness is about positions. By also queuing missing children, the traversal becomes the order of positions 1, 2, 3, … of a perfectly shaped tree. A complete tree is exactly one where, in this order, the real nodes come first and then only empty slots. A real node appearing after an empty slot means a gap.

958.takeaway: Level-order traversal that also queues missing children: a real node after the first None means the tree is not complete.
